summary: Extends the PCE Communication Protocol so a stateful PCE can ask a path computation client to hand over control of an LSP that was configured locally. The client can then delegate that LSP to the PCE, which may modify its attributes such as its path.

eli5.summary: A kid with a toy train set lets a parent take over the controls for a while. This lets a router hand control of a network path to a central planner.

questions: how does a pce request control of an lsp
what is lsp delegation in pcep
what is the pcep c flag
what does plsp-id 0 mean in pcep
subtitle: A single new flag lets a stateful PCE ask a router to hand over control of a path it configured locally.

tldr.problem: A stateful PCE can only control an LSP after the router (the PCC) delegates it, but there are cases where the PCE needs to ask for control, such as a backup PCE taking over after a failure.
tldr.mechanism: The PCE sends a PCUpd message with the new LSP Control Request flag (the C flag, bit 30 of the SRP object) set to 1, naming one LSP by PLSP-ID or all LSPs with PLSP-ID 0. The PCC decides whether to delegate.
tldr.outcome: The PCC stays the ultimate arbiter: it may grant, deny or ignore the request. A legacy PCC that does not know the flag answers with an error.

facts.label: PLSP-ID 0
facts.value: Request control of all LSPs from the PCC

today: RFC 8741 is a Proposed Standard and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It extends the stateful PCEP of RFC 8231.

sections.title: Why a PCE Needs to Ask for Control
sections.content:
RFC 8231 adds stateful operation to PCEP, the protocol between a Path Computation Client (PCC) and a Path Computation Element (PCE). It defines delegation, where a PCC grants a PCE temporary rights to modify some parameters of its LSPs, and revocation, where the PCC takes those rights back. Until now only the PCC could start a delegation.

RFC 8741 lists three cases where the PCE should be able to ask. When redundant stateful PCEs lose one member, a newly elected primary may want to take control of LSPs. When a virtualized PCE instance is started to balance load, it needs to be given some LSPs. And an operator that normally keeps control at the PCC may let the PCE take control during a global optimization run and return it afterward.
sections.eli5: Normally only the router can say "you drive this path for a while." Sometimes the planner needs to ask nicely, for example when the usual planner breaks and a backup steps in.

sections.title: The LSP Control Request Flag
sections.content:
The Stateful PCE Request Parameters (SRP) object from RFC 8231 has a Flags field. This document defines a new LSP Control Request flag, the C flag, at bit 30. A PCE sets C to 1 in a PCUpd message to say it wants control of LSPs. The LSP is named by the PLSP-ID in the LSP object that follows the SRP object. A PLSP-ID of 0 means the PCE asks for all LSPs originating from the PCC that the PCC wishes to delegate.

In other PCEP messages that carry SRP objects, C has no meaning: it MUST be set to 0 on transmission and ignored on receipt. The flag is also ignored when the R flag of RFC 8281 is set in the SRP object.
sections.eli5: It is one little checkbox on a message. When the planner ticks it, the message means "may I take over this path, please?" Writing 0 for the path number means "any path you want to hand me."

sections.title: How a Request Is Made and Answered
sections.content:
In normal delegation the PCC sets the D flag to 1 in PCRpt messages for the LSP and the PCE confirms by setting D to 1 in PCUpd messages. The PCC revokes by setting D to 0, and the PCE relinquishes the same way. To ask for control, the PCE sends a PCUpd message with C set to 1. The two flags are mutually exclusive in a PCUpd: the PCE MUST NOT send a control request for an LSP already delegated to it, and a PCC that gets both set MUST ignore C. An implementation should check the C flag before it checks the PLSP-ID.

The PCC delegates at its own discretion. If it grants or denies control it sends a PCRpt with D set to 1 or 0. It MAY also not respond, and the PCE MAY retry, preferably with an exponentially increasing timer. A control request for a non-delegated LSP MUST NOT trigger the usual error for updating a non-delegated LSP. An LSP can be delegated to only one PCE at a time, so if another PCE already holds it, the PCC MAY ignore the request or MAY revoke the first delegation first, as local policy decides.
sections.eli5: The planner asks, and the router answers yes, no, or says nothing. If the planner hears nothing, it may ask again, waiting longer each time. Only one planner can drive a path at once.

sections.title: Dealing with Legacy PCCs
sections.content:
A PCC that does not support this extension may receive a PCUpd with C set and D unset. It ignores C and treats the message as an update for a non-delegated LSP, answering with a PCErr of Error-type 19 (Invalid Operation) and error-value 1. If the PLSP-ID is 0, the error is Error-type 19 with error-value 3 (unknown PLSP-ID). A PCE therefore learns that a PCC lacks the feature only when it first asks for control.

The mechanism can be used together with RFC 8281, which describes PCE-initiated LSPs and how a PCE may take over an orphaned LSP.
sections.eli5: An older router does not know the new checkbox, so it just replies with an error. That is how the planner finds out the router is too old.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The considerations of RFC 8231 and RFC 8281 apply. The new attack vector is flooding a PCC with requests to delegate all its LSPs faster than it can process them, either by spoofing messages or by compromising the PCE. A PCC SHOULD be configured with a threshold rate for delegation requests and, when it is reached, it is RECOMMENDED to log the issue.

The PCC is the ultimate arbiter of delegation and need not trust requests blindly; it SHOULD weigh local policy before honoring one. A PCE might also face downgrade attacks by falsified error responses. As in RFC 8231, these extensions are RECOMMENDED only on authenticated and encrypted sessions between PCEs and PCCs of the same administrative authority, using TLS as in RFC 8253.
sections.eli5: A bad guy could pester the router with so many requests that it gets overwhelmed. So the router keeps a limit, writes it down when it is hit, and always decides for itself.

sections.title: Manageability and IANA
sections.content:
A PCC implementation SHOULD let the operator configure the policy for honoring control requests, including requests for an LSP delegated to another PCE, and the threshold rate for requests. A PCE implementation SHOULD allow an operator to configure the exponentially increasing retry timer. The operator MAY be able to trigger a control request for a particular LSP at the PCE. The document suggests that the PCEP YANG module could be extended to trigger such a request, and says it adds no new liveness-detection or verification requirements.

IANA allocated bit 30, "LSP Control Request", in the "SRP Object Flag Field" subregistry of the PCEP Numbers registry.
sections.eli5: The people running the network get settings to decide when the router says yes and how often the planner may ask again.

messages.label: PCUpd (C=1)
messages.note: PCE asks for control of the LSP named by PLSP-ID.

messages.label: PCRpt (D=1)
messages.note: PCC grants delegation. D=0 would deny it, or the PCC may not respond.
